country.comment: Case studies were conducted in rural and small-town communities across three districts in the Upper West Region of Ghana: Wa Municipal (Charia Water Supply System), Nadowli-Kaleo District (Nator Water Supply System) and Sissala West District (Jawia Water Supply System).

effect_estimate.comment: Primary data and analysis are purely qualitative; numeric figures reported in the paper (rural coverage rising from 27% in 1990 to 62.13% in 2017 under COM from CWSA 2017, COM tariffs up to GHS 8.0/m3, and CWSA centralised tariff of GHS 5.20/m3 as of September 2021) are descriptive institutional/secondary statistics rather than statistical effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Comparative qualitative evaluation across three water systems found that the Community Ownership and Management (COM) model promoted local participation and flexible handling of payment arrears (with secondary CWSA statistics cited showing rural coverage expanded from 27% in 1990 to 62.13% by 2017), but suffered frequent system breakdowns, unpaid volunteerism, weak District Assembly oversight, illegal connections, and revenue shortfalls despite rural tariffs reaching up to GHS 8.0/m3. Transitioning to the restructured CWSA Public Utility model improved professional staffing, maintenance, and full-cost-recovery tariff administration (centralised at GHS 5.20/m3 as of September 2021), but reduced community participation, remained vulnerable to political interference, and risked marginalising low-income residents by prioritising metered in-house connections over standpipes. The authors conclude that a Consultative (Hybrid) model—institutionalised through bylaw-backed District Water Development Boards integrating CWSA, District Assemblies, communities, and private actors—best balances technical sustainability, affordability, and inclusive governance.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed) and capped at 2 under the CODEBOOK §9 design ceiling for primary qualitative studies appraised with CASP. Through stakeholder interviews, focus groups, field observations, and policy/district documents across three water systems, the study directly documents how legal/institutional allocation of ownership and management (COM WSMTs and District Assembly trust ownership vs. CWSA professionalised utility management), tariff-setting rules, flexibility on arrears, weak regulatory enforcement, and political interference shape rural and small-town water service sustainability and access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines tariff setting and cost recovery (fees under BURDEN), WSMT flexibility toward financially disadvantaged users owing payment arrears and public standpipe provision vs. metered household connections (discretion, accommodation under DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION), community and women's representation/co-management (participation), district planning/budgeting for system expansion (planning), overlapping/shifting mandates and fragmented oversight across CWSA, GWL, District Assemblies, and WSMTs plus political interference and proposed bylaw-backed District Water Development Boards (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination), and weak bylaw/regulatory compliance oversight and illegal connections (ENFORCEMENT).
